sections.markdown:
## C — Signs: what each family of Wisconsin road signs looks like and what it requires, from yellow warning diamonds and red regulatory signs to orange work-zone, green and brown guide, blue service, route marker and railroad crossing signs
Knowledge domain: reading road signs by color, shape and symbol and knowing the action each one demands — the material behind the separate Wisconsin highway signs test and many knowledge test questions. Facts come only from the printed sign descriptions, never from the pictures.

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
When a police officer, school crossing guard or other worker directs traffic with a sign, you must obey that person even if a traffic light or road sign says something different. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
Warning signs are yellow with black words or symbols, most are diamond shaped, and they alert you to a hazard or special situation ahead. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
A Divided Highway sign means opposing lanes ahead will be separated by a physical barrier such as a guardrail. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
A Slippery When Wet sign means the pavement ahead may be slick, so reduce your speed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
A Signal Ahead sign warns of traffic lights ahead, so be prepared to slow and stop. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
A Deer Crossing sign marks an area where deer very often cross the road, so stay alert. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A01
A Lane Ends sign shows which lane is ending; move into the remaining lane once it is safe. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0026]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A02
A 2-Way Traffic sign appears where a one-way road ends and you enter a road carrying traffic in both directions. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A02
A Stop Ahead sign shows an arrow with a stop-sign shape beneath it and tells you to slow so you can stop safely at the stop sign ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A02
A Roundabout Ahead sign is a diamond with a counterclockwise symbol above a rectangular plaque reading Roundabout Ahead. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A02
A Pedestrian Crossing sign has an arrow plaque below the walker symbol showing where the crossing is, and you must yield to anyone crossing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A02
School zone and school crossing signs may be fluorescent green or yellow, and you must yield to pedestrians crossing there. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0027]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A03
Regulatory signs state the rules of the road; they are square, rectangular or a special shape and white or red with black, red, white or green lettering. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A03
A Do Not Enter sign means you may not go in; it is posted on one-way streets and on exit ramps facing the wrong direction. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A03
A Speed Limit sign gives the highest speed allowed when driving conditions are good. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A03
A Reduced Speed Ahead sign tells you to slow down, for example because a slippery road may lie ahead. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A03
On a school zone speed limit sign, the posted speed may not be exceeded whenever children can be seen. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A03
A Keep Right sign means a traffic island or other obstacle divides the road ahead. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A03
On a roundabout lane-use sign, the dot on the left-turn arrow stands for the center of the roundabout and the lines show the separate lanes. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0028]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A04
A Stop sign has eight sides and is red with white letters; come to a full stop and wait until your path is clear before going on. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A04
A Slow Moving Vehicle emblem is a triangle with reflective orange markings, and the vehicle carrying it may be moving at 25 mph or less. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A04
A Yield sign is a red and white triangle pointing down with red letters, and it means you must give the right-of-way to other vehicles. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A04
A No Passing Zone sign is a yellow pennant with black letters, and you may not pass any vehicle within that zone. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A04
A reserved parking space may be used only by a vehicle with a valid disabled parking identification permit or a valid disabled license plate. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A05
Construction signs are orange diamonds or rectangles with black letters and symbols that warn of construction, maintenance or emergency workers on or near the road. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A05
Orange signs, cones and flags around a work area are your cue to slow down. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A05
Traffic fines are doubled in construction work areas. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A05
In a construction zone you may use a cellphone only to report an emergency. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A05
A Road Construction Flagger Ahead sign warns of a worker with a sign or flag, and you must follow that worker's directions. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A05
Road Workers Ahead and Road Work Ahead signs both call for you to slow down or move over, and the Road Work Ahead sign says how far away the work is. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A06
Destination signs are square or rectangular, green or brown with white letters, and give directions and distances to places such as cities, states, airports, parks, historical sites and museums. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A06
On an Exit sign the arrow shows which side of the road the exit is on. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A06
A roundabout exit sign tells you which road you will be on after leaving the roundabout at each exit. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A06
Street name signs stand on almost every corner, mounted on top of a silver pole that faces the road they name. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A06
Brown destination signs point to recreational or scenic places, and some list the miles to get there. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A07
Service signs are square or rectangular, blue with white letters or symbols, and guide you to nearby services such as camping or a hospital. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A07
Mile markers, also called reference markers, are tall, thin blue or green signs with white letters that show where you are on the road and help emergency crews reach highway incidents faster. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A07
Each mile marker gives the travel direction, route number and mile number, and markers are spaced every one to two-tenths of a mile on the right side of the road or in the median. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A08
Route number signs change shape and color with the type of road and help you follow a route to your destination. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A08
An Interstate highway sign is a shield, red on top and blue on the bottom, with white lettering. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F41 | anchor: A09
Never race a train to a crossing, never stop on the tracks, and do not start across unless there is room for your vehicle on the far side. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F42 | anchor: A09
Do not change gears while you are crossing railroad tracks, and look both ways before crossing even when the crossing lights are not flashing. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F43 | anchor: A09
Trains are big and heavy and travel faster than they appear to. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F44 | anchor: A09
The railroad advance warning sign is round and yellow with an X symbol and black letters, telling you a crossing is ahead and to watch for a train. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F45 | anchor: A09
At a crossbuck with flashing lights, the lights flash when a train approaches from either direction; wait until they stop and the track is clear before going. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F46 | anchor: A09
A white X-shaped crossbuck with a Yield sign mounted below it means you must yield to any train using the crossing. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0034]

FACT_ID: sec05-F47 | anchor: A10
A blue Report Problem or Emergency sign with white letters stands at every highway-railroad crossing and lists a phone number for reporting a stalled vehicle on the tracks or a failed warning light. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F48 | anchor: A10
Some crossings with more than one track post a number-of-tracks sign, but not all do, so always check for additional tracks before you cross. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F49 | anchor: A10
A railroad gate comes down when a train approaches; never drive around it or under it while it is moving up or down. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F50 | anchor: A10
Where a crossing has a bell or horn with its lights, do not cross until the sound has stopped. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0035]

Misconceptions: a worker or officer directing traffic outranks the light or sign, not the other way around; the speed limit is a maximum for good conditions, not a speed you are owed in bad weather; a crossing whose lights are dark still needs a look both ways; a missing number-of-tracks sign does not prove there is only one track; a work zone allows phone use only to report an emergency.
Mnemonics: yellow warns, red and white rules, orange means workers, green and brown guide you, blue serves you; eight sides means stop, an upside-down triangle means yield, a pennant means no passing, an orange triangle means slow mover; badge for U.S., milk jug for state, red-and-blue shield for interstate.
Glossary: regulatory sign means a sign stating a rule you must obey; warning sign means a yellow sign alerting you to a hazard ahead; crossbuck means the X-shaped railroad crossing sign; pennant means the sideways triangle used for no passing zones; flagger means a work-zone worker directing traffic with a sign or flag; reference marker means a mile marker sign.
Dynamic facts: the distance on a Road Work Ahead sign and the miles on a brown destination sign change from sign to sign, so read the value posted rather than memorizing one.
